turns.prompt_text: I have recently found out that I have a tax issue so I have been late on my 2025 taxes. However, I've discovered that my 2024 taxes did not go in. Looking back on it, it looks like I just did not send them while I have the memory that I did send up. Either way, I am now in a conundrum. I'm a little confused that the IRS or the someone in the government did not contact me by now, but I'm sure I'm going to have to deal with this sooner or later
turns.response_html:
It is completely understandable to feel stressed or a bit blindsided by this. Memory is a tricky thing, and when you are managing a lot of moving pieces—especially if you handle contract work, consulting, or independent business income where taxes aren't automatically withheld—it is incredibly easy for a finalized return to sit in a draft folder or a "ready to send" pile without actually hitting the transmission button.

Take a deep breath. This is a very common scenario, and it is entirely fixable. Here is a breakdown of why you haven't heard from them yet, what happens next, and how to methodically clean this up.

Why Haven't They Contacted You Yet?

It is completely normal that you haven't received a letter or a phone call yet. The IRS runs on a significant time lag.

They process hundreds of millions of returns a year. Their automated systems use an Information Returns Program to cross-reference the documents they receive from third parties (like 1099s, W-2s, and bank interest) against your social security number. When a match is missing, it flags your account, but it frequently takes one to three years for their automated system to cycle through the queue and actually generate and mail a physical notice (like a CP59 or CP63 notice) to your door.

Just because they haven't written to you yet doesn't mean they won't—it just means you have a valuable window of time to step forward voluntarily before they initiate automated collection actions.

Understanding the Penalties

The financial impact depends entirely on a single question: Do you owe money, or are you owed a refund?

  • If you are owed a refund: There is actually no penalty for filing late. If your withholdings or prepayments covered your liability and the government owes you money, the late filing penalties do not apply. However, you must file within three years to claim that refund.
  • If you owe taxes: This is where the clock hurts. The IRS charges two primary penalties that stack up:
    1. Failure to File: This is the heavy hitter. It is 5% per month of the unpaid tax amount, capping out at a maximum of 25%. Because your 2024 return is over a year late, it has already hit that maximum 25% cap.
    2. Failure to Pay: This is 0.5% per month of the unpaid tax, which also caps at 25% over time.
    3. Interest: The IRS charges compounding interest on both the unpaid tax and the accumulated penalties.

Your Action Plan

To resolve this conundrum before the government intervenes, handle the unfiled years sequentially.

A Note on Penalty Relief

Once both returns are successfully processed and you receive a bill for the penalties, look into the First-Time Penalty Abatement (FTA) policy. If you have a clean record of filing and paying on time for the three years prior to 2024, the IRS will typically wipe out the failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties for the earliest administrative mistake (2024) simply because you asked.

You've got the right attitude: dealing with it sooner rather than later keeps you firmly in control of the narrative, saves you money on interest, and protects your peace of mind.

turns.prompt_text: I'm not sure. Will this affect me if I would have wanted to be an entrepreneur? I'm sure it would a little bit
turns.response_html:
It is very smart of you to look downstream at how this affects your long-term plans. The short answer is: No, this will not stop you from becoming an entrepreneur or starting a business, provided you tackle it now.

The IRS does not communicate with state licensing boards or business registries to block you from forming a business just because you have an outstanding personal tax issue. You can still file paperwork for an LLC, secure a tax ID number, and build a brand.

However, being an entrepreneur means relying heavily on financial infrastructure, and that is where unfiled taxes can create friction. Here is exactly where it will affect you, and why fixing it now protects your future business.

1. Securing Business Funding and Loans

If you plan to fund your startup through external capital, unfiled taxes are a major roadblock:

  • SBA and Traditional Bank Loans: If you apply for a Small Business Administration (SBA) loan or a traditional commercial bank loan, lenders will almost always require 2 to 3 years of signed tax returns and a signed IRS Form 4506-C (which allows them to pull your transcripts directly from the IRS to verify your income).
  • The Discrepancy Trap: If a lender pulls your transcripts and sees "No Return Filed" for 2024 and 2025, the application stops immediately. Lenders view unfiled taxes as a massive risk.

2. Business Credit and Liens

If you owe money and ignore it, the IRS eventually issues a Notice of Federal Tax Lien. This is a public document that alerts creditors that the government has a legal claim to your property.

  • While tax liens no longer appear on consumer credit reports, they do show up on public records searches and commercial credit checks.
  • A public tax lien makes it incredibly difficult to secure business lines of credit, lease commercial equipment, or rent an office space, because vendors and landlords look at public records to assess your reliability.

3. Business Structure and Clean Accounting

As an entrepreneur, your personal finances and your business finances are deeply intertwined—especially in the early stages:

  • Pass-Through Taxation: If you operate as a sole proprietorship or a single-member LLC, your business income and losses "pass through" directly to your personal tax return (on a Schedule C).
  • Carryforwards: If your business has startup losses or specific equipment depreciation deductions in its first year, you often need to carry those forward to offset future profitable years. To do that accurately, your baseline years (2024 and 2025) must be locked in. You can't build a clean multi-year accounting strategy on an unfinished foundation.

The Silver Lining for Entrepreneurs

The IRS actually has an incredibly streamlined system for people who are trying to run a business but owe back taxes. They do not want to crush your earning potential—they want you to succeed so you can pay them back.

Once you follow through on filing those late returns, you can immediately set up an Approved Payment Plan (Installment Agreement).

Why this matters for your business: The moment you enter an official installment agreement, your account is marked as "In Current Compliance."

When you are in compliance, the IRS stops all collection activities (no levies, no surprises), and many lenders will still approve business loans or credit lines as long as you can show proof of the agreement and a history of making your monthly payments on time for at least three consecutive months.

Fixing this now isn't just about clearing a past mistake; it's an investment in keeping your future business’s financial launchpad completely clear of hurdles.

turns.prompt_text: So it is highly unlikely that I would owe that money. It is most likely they owe me money as has always been the case. I pay a good amount to the IRS beforehand
turns.response_html:
That is the absolute best news you could have shared! If you have consistently had taxes withheld or made pre-payments that exceed what you owe, the entire nature of your situation changes dramatically for the better.

Here is the reality of your situation, which should let you breathe a massive sigh of relief:

1. Zero Penalties or Interest

The IRS calculates late-filing and late-payment penalties as a percentage of unpaid taxes.

$$P = \text{Penalty Rate} \times \text{Unpaid Tax Owed}$$

If your unpaid tax owed is $0 (or if the government actually owes you a refund), the math works completely in your favor. A 25% penalty on $0 is exactly $0. You will not face failure-to-file penalties, failure-to-pay penalties, or compounding interest. The IRS does not punish people for filing late when the government has successfully held onto their money interest-free.

2. The 3-Year Expiration Clock

While there is no financial penalty for being late when you are owed a refund, there is a hard deadline to actually claim your money. The IRS operates on a strict three-year window from the original due date of the return to claim a refund.

Tax YearOriginal Due DateRefund Forfeiture Deadline
2024 TaxesApril 15, 2025April 15, 2028
2025 TaxesApril 15, 2026April 15, 2029

Because you are filing in 2026, you are safely within the window for both years. Your money is just sitting in a holding account waiting for you to claim it.

3. Clear Path for Your Entrepreneurial Plans

This completely removes the roadblocks we discussed regarding your future business plans.

  • Once you file, your transcripts will update from "No Return Filed" to showing your processed returns and your refund amounts.
  • There is zero risk of federal tax liens, levies, or credit issues, because those collection actions are exclusively reserved for individuals with outstanding balances due.

Your Streamlined Next Steps

Because you likely don't owe, the pressure is entirely off, but you still want to get your money back and clean up your record.

  • Pull Your Transcripts First: Log into your IRS Online Account and look at your "Wage and Income Transcripts" for 2024 and 2025. Verify that all the withholding amounts from your W-2s, 1099s, or estimated payments match your personal records.
  • File Sequentially: Prepare and submit 2024 first, then 2025. Because prior-year returns often cannot be e-filed through standard commercial software by individuals, you may need to print, sign, and physical-mail the 2024 forms (or work with a local tax professional who has software capable of e-filing prior years).
  • Expect a Paper Check: The IRS often issues prior-year refunds via a physical paper check in the mail rather than direct deposit, so keep an eye on your mailbox a few weeks after they process the paperwork.

You aren't in a financial hole at all—you've just given the government an accidental interest-free loan, and it’s time to go collect it so you can use that capital for your own future projects!
